A student file is R code, and R code can change how other R code behaves.
This article shows what corrector does about that, which engine to pick, and
how to write tests that are hard to fool.

## What each engine stops

With the `callr` and `inproc` engines the tests run in the same R process as
the student code. corrector blocks the common tricks there:

- A student object that redefines a base function the tests use (`all()`,
  `==`, `isTRUE()`, testthat's `expect_equal()`, and so on) is not visible to
  the tests.
- Student S3 methods for the comparison generics (`Ops`, `==`, `all.equal`,
  `as.logical`, ...) are not visible to the tests either.
- Functions written into the global environment are not visible to the
  tests.
- `quit()` raises an error.

Allow a name with `allow_masking` when the exercise asks for it, for example
`allow_masking = "Ops.dinero"` for an exercise about an S3 class.

A student who knows R well can still get around this, because their code can
change the process itself: `attach()` a fake `isTRUE()`, register an S3
method with `registerS3method()`, or replace a base function with
`unlockBinding()`. On these engines such code is reported (see below), but it
can still change the grade.

`engine = "isolated"` closes that gap. The tests run in one R process and the
student code in another. Each student function the tests call runs in the
student process, and only its result comes back, as plain data. Nothing the
student does to their own process reaches the process that compares the
values. A student function that returns a function, an environment or an R
expression gets an `error`, because those could carry code back.

```r
results <- grade_submissions("submissions/", test_dir = "tests/",
                             engine = "isolated", workers = 4)
```

The cost is time: each exercise starts two R processes. On one machine, 10
students with 5 tests each took 9 s with `callr` and 20 s with `isolated`,
both with one worker. `workers` runs students in parallel on either engine.

## Reading the notes

On every engine, corrector reads each student file before running it and
reports calls such as `attach()`, `unlockBinding()`, `registerS3method()`,
`trace()` or `parse(text = )`, and writes into the global or base
environment, as `suspicious code: ...` in the `message` column. After the
code runs, it reports what actually changed (attached environments,
registered S3 methods, replaced base functions) as `tampering: ...`.
`scan_code()` runs the first check on its own.

The notes do not change a test's status. `grade_report()` lists the students
who got one under "Check by hand", so you can read those files yourself:

```r
grade_report(results)
#> ...
#> Check by hand (suspicious code or tampering, see the message column):
#>   Lopez
```

## Tests that are hard to fool

These habits help on every engine. They stop the S3 method tricks even on
`callr` and `inproc`. They do not stop `attach()` or replaced base functions
there (a student can attach a fake `identical()` too); only the isolated
engine stops those.

Compare with `identical()`. It does not dispatch on the class of its
arguments, and it compares the class too, so a student object with its own
`==` or `all.equal()` method does not pass:

```r
test_ejercicio1_raices <- function() {
  identical(ceros_cuadratica(1, 0, -1), c(-1, 1))
}
```

For numbers that need a tolerance, check that the result is a plain number
before you compare it:

```r
test_ejercicio1_media <- function() {
  x <- media(c(1, 2, 4))
  is.double(x) && !is.object(x) && isTRUE(all.equal(x, 7 / 3))
}
```

With testthat, prefer `expect_identical()` and `expect_type()`.

Use inputs the student cannot know in advance. A student who has seen the
tests can hard-code the answers; random inputs checked against a reference
solution in the test file stop that:

```r
test_ejercicio2_ordenar <- function() {
  x <- sample(100, 20)
  identical(ordenar(x), sort(x))
}
```

## What is still possible

- Student code runs as your user, so it can read any file you can,
  including the test files and the reference solutions in them. Run
  corrector inside a container or a virtual machine that holds only the
  submissions and the tests, and treat test files as visible to students.
- A student function returns whatever its author wants. If the tests use
  fixed inputs, an answer table works; random inputs stop that.
- The checks above look for known tricks. Obfuscated code that hides them
  usually shows up as `suspicious code` (for example a call to `parse(text = )`
  or a suspicious name inside a string), but not always.

corrector is not a sandbox. The [security notes](https://anevolbap.github.io/corrector/#security)
in the README say more.
